analysis.one_liner: Requires rear, side, and front underride guards on large trucks and trailers so cars can't slide underneath in crashes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019, despite 9 House sponsors and cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Large trucks and trailers sit higher than cars, and in a collision a car can slide underneath — an "underride" crash that often shears off the car's roof. The bill ordered the Transportation Department to write rules requiring rear, side, and front underride guards on most trucks and trailers, to make owners retrofit older trailers, and to keep guards maintained through inspections. It also required public reporting of underride crash victims. The House Transportation Committee received the bill, sent it to a subcommittee, and never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who rides in a passenger car. NHTSA has reported hundreds of preventable deaths and life-threatening injuries from underride crashes, and the bill's guards were designed to be proven in 35 mph crash tests, including partial-overlap impacts that today's rear guards often fail.

how_it_helps.text: Requires rear underride guards on trailers, semi-trailers, and single unit trucks over 10,000 pounds that pass 35 mph crash tests at center, 50%, and 30% overlap — stricter than the existing rear-guard standard.
Requires side underride guards on all covered trailers and trucks, closing the most common gap in side-impact underride crashes.
Requires front underride guards on commercial motor vehicles after DOT completes research on preventing trucks from overriding passenger cars.
Requires retrofitting older trailers and trucks with guards, plus periodic inspections, post-crash repairs, driver pre-trip inspections, and out-of-service orders for damaged guards.
Creates a Committee on Underride Protection that includes crash victims' family members and requires DOT to publish quarterly data on underride crash victims on a public website.

analysis.who_pays: Trucking companies and trailer manufacturers, who would bear the cost of designing, installing, retrofitting, and inspecting guards across new and existing trailers and trucks over 10,000 pounds. Those costs would ultimately flow through freight prices to shippers and consumers.

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates retrofitting the existing fleet of trailers and trucks built before the new rules, a substantial one-time equipment cost for carriers large and small.
It adds ongoing compliance work for carriers: periodic inspections, post-accident inspections, driver pre-trip checks, fines, and out-of-service orders for trucks with damaged guards.
Side guards add weight to trailers, which can trim payload and fuel economy — a real cost an honest supporter would weigh against the lives saved.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case is strong: NHTSA reported hundreds of preventable deaths and the NTSB had already recommended rear, side, and front guards, so the benefits were documented before the bill was written. The costs are real but conventional for vehicle safety regulation — phased compliance dates and up to 2-3 year phase-ins were built into the bill to soften them. The main honest objection is cost to smaller carriers and the weight penalty from side guards; the main criticism of the bill itself is that Congress dictated specific crash-test numbers rather than letting DOT set them.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in December 2017, it was sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which referred it to its Highways and Transit Subcommittee; neither body ever held a markup or vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on December 12, 2017, with Rep. Mark DeSaulnier as the original cosponsor.
Eight Democratic cosponsors joined; no Republican did.
The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on December 12, 2017, and to its Highways and Transit Subcommittee the next day.
No further action was taken — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Trucking companies and trailer manufacturers are better off because the equipment, retrofit, and inspection requirements never moved. Passenger vehicle occupants gained nothing: the underride hazard the bill targeted remains unaddressed by the rules this bill would have forced.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.role: Sponsor, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, named in memory of victims of underride crashes including the Karth sisters, and issued introductory remarks.

for.name: Rep. Mark DeSaulnier
for.what_they_did: Joined Cohen in introducing the bill on the day it was filed.

for.name: 8 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

for.name: National Transportation Safety Board
for.what_they_did: Had recommended installation of rear, side, and front underride guards on tractor-trailers, the recommendation the bill implements.

for.name: Families of underride crash victims
for.what_they_did: Pushed for the legislation; the bill names more than two dozen victims, including AnnaLeah and Mary Karth, and reserves two seats for victims' family members on its oversight committee.

for.name: Insurance Institute for Highway Safety
for.what_they_did: Publicly advocated for stronger underride guard standards, including side guards, through its crash testing.

against.name: Rep. Bill Shuster
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired received the bill, referred it to subcommittee, and never scheduled a markup or vote in the thirteen months remaining in the Congress.

against.name: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: American Trucking Associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed broad underride guard mandates on cost grounds, arguing requirements like side guards were expensive and of unproven benefit.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, while Republicans held the House majority and the Transportation Committee chairmanship; the bill never reached a floor vote where partisanship could be measured.

industries.note: Carriers would pay to install and retrofit guards and to run the inspections the bill requires, costs that flow into freight prices. Their interest in avoiding those costs runs against the crash protection the bill offered car occupants.

New trailers, semi-trailers, and single unit trucks over 10,000 pounds would have to be built with rear, side, and front guards meeting specified crash tests. The industry's cost of redesign runs against the public's interest in survivable crashes.

The bill would create a guaranteed market for compliant guards, including a DOT request for prototypes of high-capacity rear barriers rated to 65 mph. Their business grows only if ordinary drivers get the protection.
